questions.q: Why can an out-of-date architecture diagram be worse than having no diagram at all?
options: Because cloud providers charge extra for storing old diagrams
Because outdated diagrams always fail to open in diagramming software
Because it's trusted by default, even though it no longer reflects reality once subnets or resources have changed
Because no diagram is ever better than any diagram in practice
questions.explain: An out-of-date diagram actively misleads people who assume it's still accurate, which is more dangerous than knowing nothing exists.

questions.q: What does this lesson mean by 'access and permissions documented and transferred'?
options: Only documenting access matters; actually granting it is optional
Access only needs to be transferred for monitoring tools, not the environment itself
The new owner's access must actually be granted, not just described on paper
Permissions should never be written down for security reasons
questions.explain: A handoff where the new owner can read about access but can't actually log in and act isn't a real handoff.

questions.q: Why does the checklist include updating monitoring and alerting contacts?
options: Because monitoring contacts have no real effect on incident response
Because alerts are automatically reassigned when an employee leaves
Because this item only matters for environments without a runbook
Because an alert still pointed at someone who's leaving goes nowhere useful or to someone who can't act on it
questions.explain: If alert contacts aren't updated, a real incident can page someone who is no longer available or responsible, delaying response.

questions.q: Why does the checklist call for noting known issues and technical debt during a handoff?
options: Because technical debt must be fixed before any handoff can occur
Because listing technical debt is a legal requirement for cloud deployments
Because known issues are purely cosmetic and don't affect operations
So the new owner inherits known problems explicitly instead of discovering them mid-incident and assuming they broke something themselves
questions.explain: Naming rough edges up front means the new owner isn't blindsided by a pre-existing problem during a live incident.

questions.q: How does this lesson say the handoff checklist should be treated?
options: As a gate, like a pre-flight checklist — if any item is unchecked, the handoff isn't actually done yet
As a checklist only relevant to disaster recovery, not everyday handoffs
As an optional formality to sign quickly on the way out the door
As a one-time task that never needs to be repeated for future handoffs
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly compares it to a pre-flight checklist: an unchecked item means the handoff isn't finished, the same bar Lesson 21 set for a deployment itself.
